metadata.source: Corrective exercise triage framework. Content based on public-domain and peer-reviewed assessments and rehabilitation literature (e.g. Cook FMS, Kendall, McGill, Kibler, Silfverskiöld, Thomas test variants, PNF Knott-Voss). Scope consistent with corrective exercise practice.
metadata.description: Clinical cases for progressive triage - identification of signs and decision

levels.training: Guided - Category indicators are shown on signs
levels.practice: Practice - Only some indicators are visible
levels.evaluation: Evaluation - No hints, as in real life

signCategories.green: Favorable signs - indicate you can train

cases.title: Postural low back pain in office worker
cases.scenario: 34-year-old female client presents with low back pain for 3 weeks that worsens at the end of the workday. She works 8 hours seated at a computer. Started running 2 months ago (3x/week). No specific trauma remembered.

signs.text: Pain 4/10 at rest, 6/10 after prolonged sitting

cases.reasoning: This case shows a classic MECHANICAL low back pain pattern associated with postural dysfunction. Key findings: no radiation (rules out radiculopathy), full mobility, normal strength and reflexes (no neurologic deficit), and an identifiable postural pattern. NO red flags.

cases.title: Low back pain with leg radiation
cases.scenario: 52-year-old male client presents with low back pain radiating to the glute and posterior right thigh for 6 weeks. Started after lifting a heavy suitcase. Improves somewhat with anti-inflammatories. History of similar episodes 5 and 8 years ago.

signs.text: Positive straight leg raise at 45 deg right

cases.reasoning: Findings suggest lumbar RADICULOPATHY (L5-S1). The presence of OBJECTIVE NEUROLOGIC DEFICIT (strength 4/5 and decreased reflex) requires referral. IMPORTANT: absence of cauda equina signs (sphincter control OK) means it is not urgent.
keyPoints: Objective neurologic deficit requires medical evaluation
NO cauda equina signs = not urgent
approach: After medical evaluation: progressive neural mobilization

cases.title: Night low back pain in smoker
cases.scenario: 67-year-old male client with progressive low back pain for 2 months that does not improve with rest or changing positions. Pain is constant, even at night, waking him at 3-4am. Smoker of 40 pack-years. History of prostate cancer treated 4 years ago.

signs.text: Night pain that wakes the patient
Unintentional weight loss (8 kg in 2 months)
No improvement with rest or position changes

cases.reasoning: MULTIPLE RED FLAGS for MALIGNANT PATHOLOGY: constant night pain, unintentional weight loss, cancer history (prostate commonly metastasizes to bone), non-mechanical pain. URGENT referral to rule out metastasis.
keyPoints: Non-mechanical night pain = major red flag
Weight loss + cancer history = suspicion of malignancy

cases.title: Impingement in a crossfitter

patient.profile: Female, 28 years old, programmer and crossfitter

cases.scenario: 28-year-old female client with anterior right shoulder pain for 3 weeks, especially during overhead exercises. Trains CrossFit 5x/week. Pain started gradually without direct trauma. No significant night pain.
cases.reasoning: Findings are consistent with mild SUBACROMIAL IMPINGEMENT associated with scapulothoracic dysfunction. Positive Hawkins-Kennedy and typical painful arc. ABSENCE of red flags: no trauma, no night pain, no instability, near-normal strength.
keyPoints: No red flags - manageable with correctives

cases.title: Mechanical knee locking
cases.scenario: 45-year-old male client with right knee pain for 4 weeks. Stands 10h/day at work. No clear trauma. Reports episodes where the knee "locks" in flexion and must be manually moved to unlock. Intermittent swelling.
cases.reasoning: Findings suggest a MENISCAL LESION: mechanical locking is pathognomonic, positive McMurray, joint line pain, effusion. Requires MRI to confirm and determine treatment.
keyPoints: McMurray + joint line pain = high suspicion
Stable ligaments are good but do not rule out meniscus

cases.title: Cauda equina syndrome
cases.scenario: 38-year-old female client with severe low back pain of sudden onset 2 days ago during deadlift. Pain 9/10 that does not improve. Since yesterday, difficulty urinating (needs to strain) and numbness in the perineal area.

signs.text: Very positive straight leg raise bilaterally

cases.reasoning: NEUROSURGICAL EMERGENCY: CAUDA EQUINA SYNDROME. Triad present: saddle anesthesia, bladder dysfunction, bilateral motor deficit. Urgent surgical decompression in <24-48h. CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES.
keyPoints: Cauda triad: perineal anesthesia + bladder dysfunction + motor deficit
Do not wait - call emergency services immediately
approach: DO NOTHING ELSE - CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES

cases.title: Postural neck tension
cases.scenario: 22-year-old male client with neck pain and stiffness for 1 week, worse on the right side. Spent many hours studying on a laptop with poor posture. Pain improves with heat and movement. No prior trauma.

signs.text: Limited cervical ROM to right rotation
Normal strength and reflexes in upper limbs

cases.reasoning: TYPICAL picture of postural cervical muscle tension. Trigger points, clear postural pattern (FHP + kyphosis), improves with movement, and NO neurologic signs. Ideal CES case.
keyPoints: Mechanical pain: improves with movement = benign
approach: Chin tucks for deep neck flexors

cases.title: Classic lateral epicondylitis
cases.scenario: 48-year-old female client with right elbow and forearm pain for 6 weeks. Began with intensive mouse use during accounting close. Pain with gripping. No trauma.
cases.reasoning: Classic LATERAL EPICONDYLITIS (tennis elbow). Specific tests positive (Cozen, Mill), typical location, overuse pattern, no neurologic signs. Tendinopathy that responds well to eccentric exercise.
keyPoints: Full ROM and no neurologic signs

cases.title: Myelopathy in immunosuppressed

patient.profile: Male, 71 years old, retired with COPD

cases.scenario: 71-year-old male client with constant mid-back pain and progressive leg weakness over the last 3 weeks. Walking is increasingly difficult. Uses chronic inhaled and oral steroids for severe COPD. Intermittent low-grade fever (37.5-38 C).
cases.reasoning: SUSPECTED SPINAL INFECTION with MYELOPATHY. Fever + vertebral pain + UPPER MOTOR NEURON SIGNS (hyperreflexia, Babinski) indicate spinal cord compression. Immunosuppression increases risk. Urgent MRI.
keyPoints: Fever + spinal pain + immunosuppression = infection until proven otherwise

cases.title: Chronic ankle instability
cases.scenario: 40-year-old female client reports left ankle instability with recurrent sprains (3 in the last year). First severe sprain was 3 years ago. Currently no pain. The ankle "gives way" on uneven surfaces.
cases.reasoning: CHRONIC ANKLE INSTABILITY post-sprain. No acute injury; problem is proprioceptive deficit and weakness. Neuromuscular training has excellent evidence and is the treatment of choice.
keyPoints: No acute injury = safe to train
Functional instability responds very well to exercise
Proprioceptive deficit and weakness = clear targets

cases.title: Suspected rotator cuff tear
cases.scenario: 55-year-old male client with right shoulder pain for 3 months after a fall on an outstretched arm. Significant night pain that wakes him. Progressive difficulty lifting the arm and combing hair. Works painting ceilings.

signs.text: Positive empty can test with weakness

cases.reasoning: Multiple signs suggest ROTATOR CUFF TEAR: positive drop arm and lag sign (specific), significant weakness, visible atrophy, trauma + age >50. Imaging required to decide treatment.
keyPoints: Drop arm + lag sign = high specificity for tear
approach: Depends on tear size on imaging

cases.title: Inflammatory low back pain
cases.scenario: 26-year-old female client with low back and bilateral glute pain for 8 months. Morning stiffness lasting >1 hour and improves with activity. Wakes at 4-5am due to pain. Improves significantly with ibuprofen. Brother has psoriasis.
cases.reasoning: Profile of INFLAMMATORY LOW BACK PAIN. Meets criteria: prolonged morning stiffness, improves with exercise and NSAIDs, night pain, family history of autoimmunity. Possible SPONDYLOARTHROPATHY. Requires rheumatologic evaluation.
keyPoints: Inflammatory pain != mechanical pain (improves with movement)
Family history of autoimmunity is relevant
approach: After rheumatology diagnosis: exercise is ESSENTIAL

cases.title: Plantar fasciitis in recreational runner
cases.scenario: 29-year-old runner reports heel pain for 6 weeks. Pain is worst with the first steps in the morning and after long periods of sitting. He recently increased weekly mileage and started hill training. No trauma reported.

signs.text: Heel pain with first steps in the morning
Tenderness at the medial calcaneal tubercle

cases.reasoning: Presentation is consistent with mechanical plantar fasciitis: morning start-up pain, load-related symptoms, and no red flags. Safe to train with load management and corrective focus.
keyPoints: No neurological or inflammatory red flags
approach: Reduce running volume and avoid hills temporarily

cases.title: Patellofemoral pain in gym member
cases.scenario: 22-year-old female reports anterior knee pain for 2 months, worse with stairs, squats, and long sitting. She recently added more plyometrics to her training. No trauma or swelling reported.

signs.text: Anterior knee pain with stairs and squats
Dynamic knee valgus on single-leg squat

cases.reasoning: Pattern aligns with mechanical patellofemoral pain. No instability, swelling, or trauma. Safe to train with technique work and load adjustment.
keyPoints: Movement quality and load management are central
